Subject: Follow-up from today — latency targets and concurrency

Marissa,

Thanks for the product demo this morning — appreciated the overview on the streaming path and KV cache behavior. A quick recap from our side and a few clarifying questions before we loop Legal/Procurement:

- SLOs: We need 95th pct response time <= 350ms for our primary chat flow (max tokens: 256).
- Throughput: steady-state 1,500 reqs/min for US region.
- Concurrency: burst concurrency up to 1,200 parallel requests during business hours (10am–6pm), with connection pooling (keep-alive) from our side.
- Streaming: we will use streaming for real-time assistant; perceived latency is critical.

Questions:
1) Does Redwood recommend a single model variant for this workload or a fallback variant for spikes?
2) What are the practical rate limits/quotas we should propose in the PO to avoid throttling?

Attaching a sample load profile (acme_load_profile.csv).

Next steps: If we can get an updated quota proposal and a short note on fallback behavior, I can push to Procurement early next week.

Thanks,
John
Director, Platform Integrations
Acme Corp

John — thanks for the clear recap and the CSV. Quick answers inline and proposal attached.

1) Model variants / fallback: For the 95p<=350ms target with a 256-token median, we recommend using the rwd-mid-std model as primary and rwd-mid-fast as an automated fallback during capacity-constrained windows. The runtime will auto-route based on latency SLO policy; fallback is per-request and preserves API semantics.

2) Rate limits / quotas: based on your steady 1,500 reqs/min and 1,200 burst concurrency, our recommendation is:
   - Provisioned concurrency quota: 1,200 concurrent slots (reserved)
   - Rate limit: 10,000 requests/min (headroom for retries and non-chat traffic)
   - Streaming token throughput: 150k tokens/min aggregated

We attached redwood_concurrency_pricing_v2.pdf with a pricing line for reserved concurrency and an SLO addendum that includes our auto-fallback behavior and a one-time quota bump process.

Technical note: connection pooling with keep-alive is supported; we recommend HTTP/2 multiplexing where possible. We also suggest enabling prefix caching for repeated prompts to reduce per-token cost.

If that aligns, I can prepare a one-page statement of work for Procurement and an intake doc for our Dedicated capacity onboarding.

Best,
Marissa
Enterprise AE | Redwood Inference

John — quick technical follow-up from Engineering: a few clarifications to make sure the quota mapping is correct.

- When you say 1,200 parallel requests, do you mean 1,200 concurrent open HTTP connections or 1,200 concurrent active inference slots (i.e., in-flight tokens)? For autoscaling and reserved capacity we treat "concurrency slots" as active model execution contexts (in-flight).
- If your clients use HTTP/2 multiplexing with long-lived connections, the connection count will be much lower; we only need to count in-flight requests for quota consumption.

Proposal refinement: reserve 1,200 concurrency slots and request a soft rate-limit of 12,000 reqs/min to account for retries and background calls. That keeps headroom without overcommitting on provisioned GPUs.

Logan
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Marissa / Logan — thanks, this is helpful. Quick answers:
- We mean 1,200 in-flight inference slots. Our client does use HTTP/2 mux in most places but some legacy clients are short-lived connections.
- Streaming is used for ~60% of requests; tokens/min numbers in the sample profile reflect that.

Procurement asked whether Redwood can guarantee no throttling for production with the reserved concurrency. Also asked for a one-line clause they can include in the PO re: temporary quota bumps for seasonal spikes.

Can you provide: (a) a 1–2 sentence commitment on throttling behavior with reserved concurrency, and (b) the process to request a temporary quota bump (SLA/lead time)?

Sara / John — great questions. See two-liners below you can paste into the PO + short process.

(a) Throttling commitment (1–2 lines for PO):
"With a reserved concurrency commitment of 1,200 slots, Redwood will provision capacity to keep production requests within agreed latency SLOs. Redwood will not throttle requests that fit within the reserved concurrency and configured rate limit; excess traffic will be subject to soft throttling policies described in the SLO addendum."

(b) Temporary quota bump process (short):
"Customers may request a temporary quota increase via the Redwood Console or by opening a priority support ticket. For planned spikes, request at least 72 hours in advance for a standard temporary bump (subject to capacity). For emergency/short-notice increases, Redwood will triage on a best-effort basis and can often apply short-term capacity within 6–24 hours depending on region availability. All temporary increases are logged and billed per the reserved/usage terms in the contract."
